transcript.content: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I’m constantly forgetting little everyday things—appointments, errands, even finishing what I start for the community center. My husband and friends were worried it might be early dementia, but my primary care doctor suggested it could actually be a long-standing attention problem instead, which is why I'm here to see you.
Looking back at your childhood or teenage years, do you remember struggling with focus, organization, or forgetfulness even before these recent concerns began?

Yes, these struggles actually go back to when I was quite young. On my elementary school report cards, teachers always wrote that I was bright but would "daydream, rush, and talk out of turn." My mother also used to scold me because I'd wander off halfway through my chores to do something else and never finish them.
Besides the forgetfulness and trouble focusing, do you often find yourself feeling restless, having trouble sitting still, or acting impulsively without thinking things through?

Yes, my family jokes that I can never just sit still, and during quiet times like church or movies, I get this pent-up energy that makes me fidget with my bracelet or want to get up. I also get very impatient waiting in lines, and I often impulsively interrupt or finish people's sentences during our committee meetings.

Do these difficulties with focus, restlessness, and impulsivity consistently cause significant problems in at least two areas of your life, such as at home, in social settings, or during your volunteer work?

Yes, they definitely affect both my home life and my volunteer work. At the community center, I've mixed up dates and forgotten supplies to the point where other volunteers have gently suggested I step back from leading projects. At home, I'm constantly forgetting errands and double-booking events, which is why my husband and friends got so worried that they thought I was developing dementia.
